nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the Abbey playwright of Katie Roche and the woman's Ireland
literary_identity: Playwright; the Abbey dramatist of A Disciple, The King of Spain's Daughter and Katie Roche.
biography: Born Teresa Deevy at Waterford on 21 February 1894; she lost her hearing in her nineteenth year and wrote for the Abbey from The Reapers (1930) through A Disciple (1931), The King of Spain's Daughter (1935) and Katie Roche (1936), the plays of the woman confined by the custom of the rural Ireland. Her plays left the Abbey stage after 1937 and were recovered at the end of the century; she died at Waterford on 23 April 1963.
literary_profile: Teresa Deevy is the lost playwright of the Abbey and the dramatist of the woman's Ireland: Katie Roche and The King of Spain's Daughter put the woman confined by the custom and the convent on the Abbey stage with an edge the revival did not match, and her recovery made her one of the rediscovered dramatists of the century.
stylistic_characteristics: The Abbey dialogue of the rural Ireland with the woman's confinement at its centre; the unsettling close that refuses the convention; the one-act and the three-act of the custom and the escape; the radio play of the later years; the plain speech of the serving girl and the priest.
intellectual_concerns: The woman confined by the custom and the convent; the rural Ireland of the republic; the Abbey stage and its refusal of her plays; the deafness and the theatre of the speech; the unsettling close as the moral form.
historical_significance: Teresa Deevy is the lost playwright of the Abbey and the dramatist of the woman's Ireland: Katie Roche and The King of Spain's Daughter put the confined woman on the Abbey stage with an edge the revival did not match.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the novelist of Hornblower and of the African Queen
literary_identity: Novelist; the creator of Horatio Hornblower and the author of The African Queen.
biography: Born Cecil Scott Forester at Cairo on 27 August 1899; he took to journalism and then to the novel with Payment Deferred (1926), and made his name with the sea novels - The African Queen (1935), The General (1936) and the Hornblower books from Beat to Quarters (1937). The Hornblower series made the naval novel of the Napoleonic wars one of the most read fictions of the century; he died at Fullerton, California, on 2 April 1966.
literary_profile: C. S. Forester is the creator of Horatio Hornblower and the master of the naval novel: the Hornblower books made the frigate of the Napoleonic wars the theatre of the professional conscience, The African Queen is the classic of the river pursuit, and The General is the satire of the high command of the first war.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain exact prose of the professional; the ship, the gun and the wind reported as the moral argument; the frigate and the river as the theatre of the conscience; the satire of the high command in the same plain sentence; the serial novel of the career.
intellectual_concerns: The professional conscience and the service; the Napoleonic war at sea; the river pursuit and the African war; the high command and the waste of the first war; the career as the form of the novel.
historical_significance: C. S. Forester is the creator of Horatio Hornblower and the master of the naval novel: the Hornblower books made the frigate of the Napoleonic wars the theatre of the professional conscience, and The African Queen is the classic of the river pursuit.

literary_identity: Novelist; the thriller writer of The Devil Rides Out and of the between-wars secret war.
biography: Born Dennis Yates Wheatley in London on 8 January 1897; he served in the war and in the between-wars years made the thriller of the secret war and of the occult with Forbidden Territory (1933), Black August (1934) and The Devil Rides Out (1935), and served in the war's deception planning. His output of the thriller ran to eighty volumes; he died in London on 10 November 1977.

literary_identity: Novelist; the Welsh author of O Absalom! and My Son, My Son!
biography: Born Howard Spring at Cardiff on 10 February 1889; he worked as a journalist in London and the provinces before O Absalom! (1934), the novel of the Welsh preacher and his son, made him a bestseller. My Son, My Son! (1938) and Fame Is the Spur (1940) carried the Welsh and the political novel into the war years; he moved to Cornwall and died at St Austell on 31 May 1965.

literary_identity: Novelist; the doctor-novelist of Hatter's Castle, The Stars Look Down and The Citadel.
biography: Born Archibald Joseph Cronin at Cardross, Dunbartonshire, on 19 July 1896; he practised as a doctor, including as a medical inspector of mines, before Hatter's Castle (1931) made him a novelist. The Stars Look Down (1935), The Citadel (1937) and The Keys of the Kingdom (1941) made the novel of the profession and of the mining town one of the most read fictions of the century; he died at Montreux on 6 January 1981.

literary_identity: Painter and novelist; the author of The Ragged Trousered Philanthropists.
biography: Born Robert Phillipe Noonan at Dublin on 18 April 1870; he worked as a house painter in Cape Town and Hastings and wrote The Ragged Trousered Philanthropists, the novel of the painters of the town of Mugsborough, in the years before his death. He died of tuberculosis at Liverpool on 3 February 1911, and the book was published, cut, in 1914, with the full text only in 1955.

biography: Born Margaret Storm Jameson at Whitby, Yorkshire, on 7 January 1891; she read at Leeds and the Sorbonne and published from 1922, making her name with the thirties trilogy The Mirror in Darkness - Company Parade (1934), Love Won (1935), None Turn Again (1936) - and with the criticism of the novel. As president of English PEN and as editor she shaped the reception of the exiled writers; she died in 1986.

biography: Born Phyllis Eleanor Bentley at Halifax, Yorkshire, on 19 November 1894, the daughter of a partner in a woollen mill; she taught after war work in munitions and published from 1922 with Gollancz.
